subtopics.title: Taking out a common factor
subtopics.exposition: Factorisation is the opposite process of expanding brackets. The expressions 2(x+1) and 2x+2 are equivalent: they have the same value for all values of x. Factorising based on common factors relies on there being factors common to all the terms. The taking out of common factors is the starting point in all factorisation problems. Factorisation starts with the expanded expression and ends with a bracketed one; for example, start with 2x+2 and end up with 2(x+1). The expression 2x - 6x^2 can be factorised as 2x(1 - 3x).

subtopics.title: Common binomial factor
subtopics.exposition: 2 - a = -(a - 2): switching the terms in a bracket gives the negative of the original bracket. The expression 2(x - 1) - a(x - 1) can be factorised as (x - 1)(2 - a). A "switch around" strategy is used to find the common factor when the brackets, such as (a - 2) and (2 - a), differ in sign. Writing 2 - a as -(a - 2), the expression 5(a - 2) - b(2 - a) becomes 5(a - 2) - [-b(a - 2)], which equals 5(a - 2) + b(a - 2). Taking out the common factor (a - 2) from 5(a - 2) + b(a - 2) gives (a - 2)(5 + b).

subtopics.title: Difference of two squares
subtopics.exposition: (ax + b)(ax - b) can be expanded to a^2x^2 - b^2. a^2x^2 - b^2 can be factorised as (ax + b)(ax - b). x^2 - 16 can be written as x^2 - 4^2, which is a difference of two squares. The factors of x^2 - 16 are (x - 4) and (x + 4). To spot a difference of two squares, look for an expression consisting of two terms. To spot a difference of two squares, look for terms that have different signs (one positive, one negative). To spot a difference of two squares, look for each term being a perfect square. Examples of a difference of two squares are a^2 - 1, 4x^2 - y^2 and -49 + p^4. Take out the common factor (a^2 - 4) from 3a(a^2 - 4) - 7(a^2 - 4) to get (a^2 - 4)(3a - 7). Then factorise the difference of two squares: (a^2 - 4)(3a - 7) = (a - 2)(a + 2)(3a - 7).

subtopics.title: Factorising by grouping in pairs
subtopics.exposition: Factorising a four-term expression by grouping the terms in pairs and taking out the common bracket is called factorising by grouping. The factors of 3x + 3 are 3 and (x + 1). The factors of 2x^2 + 2x are 2x and (x + 1). The expression 2x^2 + 2x + 3x + 3 has no common factor to all four terms, but it can still be factorised by grouping the terms. Group the terms in pairs and take out the common factor of each pair: (2x^2 + 2x) + (3x + 3) = 2x(x + 1) + 3(x + 1). After taking out the common factor from each pair, there is another common factor, (x + 1). Taking out the common factor (x + 1) gives (x + 1)(2x + 3). To get the second factor, take out the common bracket (x + 1) and see what is left over. What is left over is 2x from the first group and +3 from the second group. In 7x + 14y + bx + 2by, the ratio of the coefficients 7:14 is the same as b:2b, so 7 is a common factor of the first two terms and b is a common factor of the second two terms. Group terms with common factors together: 7x + 14y + bx + 2by = (7x + 14y) + (bx + 2by) = 7(x + 2y) + b(x + 2y). Take out the common factor (x + 2y): 7(x + 2y) + b(x + 2y) = (x + 2y)(7 + b). Alternatively, group x as the common factor of the first and third terms and 2y as the common factor of the second and fourth terms, where 7:b = 14:2b. Rearrange the equation with grouped terms together: 7x + 14y + bx + 2by = (7x + bx) + (14y + 2by) = x(7 + b) + 2y(7 + b). Take out the common factor (7 + b): x(7 + b) + 2y(7 + b) = (7 + b)(x + 2y). The factors of 7x + 14y + bx + 2by are (7 + b) and (x + 2y).

claims.claim: Factorisation is the opposite process of expanding brackets.
Factorisation starts with the expanded expression and ends with a bracketed one; for example, start with 2x+2 and end up with 2(x+1).
The expressions 2(x+1) and 2x+2 are equivalent: they have the same value for all values of x.
Factorising based on common factors relies on there being factors common to all the terms.
The expression 2x - 6x^2 can be factorised as 2x(1 - 3x).
The taking out of common factors is the starting point in all factorisation problems.
The expression 2(x - 1) - a(x - 1) can be factorised as (x - 1)(2 - a).
A "switch around" strategy is used to find the common factor when the brackets, such as (a - 2) and (2 - a), differ in sign.
2 - a = -(a - 2): switching the terms in a bracket gives the negative of the original bracket.
Writing 2 - a as -(a - 2), the expression 5(a - 2) - b(2 - a) becomes 5(a - 2) - [-b(a - 2)], which equals 5(a - 2) + b(a - 2).
Taking out the common factor (a - 2) from 5(a - 2) + b(a - 2) gives (a - 2)(5 + b).
(ax + b)(ax - b) can be expanded to a^2x^2 - b^2.
a^2x^2 - b^2 can be factorised as (ax + b)(ax - b).
x^2 - 16 can be written as x^2 - 4^2, which is a difference of two squares.
The factors of x^2 - 16 are (x - 4) and (x + 4).
To spot a difference of two squares, look for an expression consisting of two terms.
To spot a difference of two squares, look for terms that have different signs (one positive, one negative).
To spot a difference of two squares, look for each term being a perfect square.
Examples of a difference of two squares are a^2 - 1, 4x^2 - y^2 and -49 + p^4.
Take out the common factor (a^2 - 4) from 3a(a^2 - 4) - 7(a^2 - 4) to get (a^2 - 4)(3a - 7).
Then factorise the difference of two squares: (a^2 - 4)(3a - 7) = (a - 2)(a + 2)(3a - 7).
The factors of 3x + 3 are 3 and (x + 1).
The factors of 2x^2 + 2x are 2x and (x + 1).
The expression 2x^2 + 2x + 3x + 3 has no common factor to all four terms, but it can still be factorised by grouping the terms.
Group the terms in pairs and take out the common factor of each pair: (2x^2 + 2x) + (3x + 3) = 2x(x + 1) + 3(x + 1).
After taking out the common factor from each pair, there is another common factor, (x + 1).
Taking out the common factor (x + 1) gives (x + 1)(2x + 3).
To get the second factor, take out the common bracket (x + 1) and see what is left over.
What is left over is 2x from the first group and +3 from the second group.
Factorising a four-term expression by grouping the terms in pairs and taking out the common bracket is called factorising by grouping.
In 7x + 14y + bx + 2by, the ratio of the coefficients 7:14 is the same as b:2b, so 7 is a common factor of the first two terms and b is a common factor of the second two terms.
Group terms with common factors together: 7x + 14y + bx + 2by = (7x + 14y) + (bx + 2by) = 7(x + 2y) + b(x + 2y).
Take out the common factor (x + 2y): 7(x + 2y) + b(x + 2y) = (x + 2y)(7 + b).
Alternatively, group x as the common factor of the first and third terms and 2y as the common factor of the second and fourth terms, where 7:b = 14:2b.
Rearrange the equation with grouped terms together: 7x + 14y + bx + 2by = (7x + bx) + (14y + 2by) = x(7 + b) + 2y(7 + b).
Take out the common factor (7 + b): x(7 + b) + 2y(7 + b) = (7 + b)(x + 2y).
The factors of 7x + 14y + bx + 2by are (7 + b) and (x + 2y).
